subject: Karaca et al. (2015)
object: Karaca et al. (2015) described a male patient (BAB4453) with microcephaly, spasticity and intellectual disability. He had dysmorphic features resembling Coffin-Siris syndrome, including a coarse face, bushy eyebrows, facial hypertrichosis and long eyelashes. Brain imaging showed severe cortical atrophy. Family history was negative.

subject: Karaca et al. (2015)
object: In a male patient (BAB4453) with microcephaly, spasticity, intellectual disability and Coffin-Siris-like dysmorphic features, Karaca et al. (2015) used whole exome sequencing to identify a hemizygous null variant in the SMARCA1 gene (c.C7T, p.Q3X; NM_003069). SMARCA1 encodes a member of the SWI/SNF protein family and is part of the ATP-dependent CECR2-containing remodeling factor (CERF). A figure legend in the paper calls the same variant a homozygous stop gain.

subject: SMARCA1 c.7C>T / p.Q3*
Lopes et al. (2016)
object: Lopes et al. (2016) studied 19 Portuguese patients (16 girls and 3 boys) whose clinical presentation overlapped significantly with Rett syndrome. The patients were studied with array CGH, whole-exome sequencing, MRI and muscle biopsy.

subject: Lopes et al. (2016)
object: In a cohort of 19 Portuguese patients with Rett-like phenotypes, Lopes et al. (2016) used whole-exome sequencing to find variants in 5 novel candidate neurodevelopmental disorder genes (26% of patients). These were de novo variants in RHOBTB2, SMARCA1 and GABBR2, a homozygous variant in EIF4G1, and compound heterozygous variants in HTT. Network analysis showed that these genes interact through protein interactions with each other and with the known Rett syndrome genes.

Lopes et al. (2016)
object: Lopes et al. (2016) found variants in genes already linked to neurodevelopmental disorders in 6 of 19 patients (32%) with Rett-like phenotypes. Three patients had de novo variants in EEF1A2, STXBP1 or ZNF238. Two male patients had maternally inherited X-linked variants in SLC35A2, ZFX and SHROOM4. One patient had a homozygous EIF2B2 variant. Pathogenic genomic imbalances were found in 2 further patients: an 18q21.2 deletion that included 4 exons of TCF4, and mosaic uniparental disomy of chromosome 3.

subject: Riazuddin et al. (2017)
object: Riazuddin et al. (2017) carried out exome sequencing in 121 consanguineous Pakistani families with autosomal recessive intellectual disability. In a Siraiki Baloch family (PKMR213), they found a variant in the novel candidate gene TMEM222 (NM_032125.2), c.214G>A (p.Gly72Ser), that segregated with the phenotype. The variant had a CADD score of 34.0 and an ExAC allele frequency of 8.237 x 10(-6), and it was absent from 213 ethnically matched controls.

subject: TMEM222 c.214G>A / p.G72S
Nishimura et al. (2025)
object: Nishimura et al. (2025) reported 2 unrelated male patients with X-linked intellectual disability. Patient 1 had macrocephaly, behavioral difficulty, and learning disability; patient 2 had ataxia and speech delay.

subject: Nishimura et al. (2025)
object: In a male patient (patient 1) with X-linked intellectual disability, macrocephaly, behavioral difficulty, and learning disability, Nishimura et al. (2025) identified by exome sequencing a hemizygous nonsense variant in the SMARCA1 gene (c.1795C-T, Gln599Ter; NM_003069.5) that led to nonsense-mediated decay. The variant was inherited from his unaffected mother.

subject: SMARCA1 c.1795C>T / p.Q599*
Nishimura et al. (2025)
object: In a male patient (patient 2) with X-linked intellectual disability, ataxia, and speech delay, Nishimura et al. (2025) identified by exome sequencing a hemizygous missense variant in the SMARCA1 gene (c.1343G-T, Arg448Leu; NM_003069.5), inherited from his unaffected mother. Structural modeling suggested that Arg448Leu might destabilize interactions between SMARCA1 and nucleosomal DNA.

subject: SMARCA1 c.1343G>T / p.R448L
Nishimura et al. (2025)
object: Nishimura et al. (2025) found that the SMARCA1 variants in both affected males were inherited from unaffected healthy mothers. They suggested that hemizygous variants impairing SMARCA1 function can cause XLID with variable features in males.

subject: Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) described an X-linked neurodevelopmental disorder caused by de novo or maternally inherited SMARCA1 variants in 35 individuals from 26 families. Features ranged from mild to severe intellectual disability/developmental delay and included delayed or regressive speech, autism spectrum disorder features, facial dysmorphism and other variable features. Individuals with truncating variants had a high penetrance of macrocephaly.

subject: Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) studied a 6-generation family with 4 affected individuals who had mild to severe ID/DD and brain overgrowth. The proband, a 12-year-old boy, had head circumference (OFC) +6 SD, severe ID without language, ASD, hydrocephalus treated with a shunt, hepatosplenomegaly, and height and weight +5 SD. His brother had OFC +4.3 SD, mild ID, hydrocephalus and splenomegaly. Two maternal cousins (a 14-year-old girl and an 8-year-old boy) had OFC +4.9 and +5.5 SD, mild learning disability, obesity and normal brain MRI. Their carrier mothers had OFC +1 and +1.5 SD and no learning disability.

subject: Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: In the 4 affected members of the 6-generation family, Mirzaa et al. (2025) used exome sequencing to identify a hemizygous or heterozygous nonsense variant in SMARCA1, c.271C-T (p.Arg91Ter). Both mothers were heterozygous carriers, and the paternal grandfather and a maternal uncle did not carry the variant. The same variant was found in a second, unrelated family (family 2): a 6-year-old boy with macrocephaly, ASD and ADHD who had inherited it from his mother.

subject: SMARCA1 c.271C>T / p.R91*
Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) reported 35 affected individuals (26 males, 9 females) aged 2 to 49 years. Features were ID/DD (27/35), speech delay and/or regression (29/35), OFC of +2 SD or more and/or reported macrocephaly (17/35), motor delay (20/34), seizures (8/35), hypotonia (15/35), behavioral difficulties (19/35), ASD (11/35) and dysmorphic facial features (19/35). Height of +2 SD or more was less frequent (29%), which the authors said argued against a generalized overgrowth syndrome. Common facial features were frontal bossing, a long face, slanted palpebral fissures, a flat nasal root with a short bulbous nose, anteverted nares and a thin upper lip.

subject: Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) noted other recurring features in the cohort. These included urogenital/kidney anomalies (9 individuals), gastrointestinal problems (9), eye/vision deficits (8) and hepatomegaly/splenomegaly (3). Recurrent dysmorphic features included ear anomalies (11 individuals) and micrognathia (5).

subject: Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) reported that, of the 26 index cases, 17 had maternally inherited SMARCA1 variants and 4 had de novo variants. Segregation was not determined in 5, of which 4 were presumed maternal. Three-quarters of affected individuals were hemizygous males; heterozygous females made up 25% and often had milder phenotypes, consistent with X-linked inheritance.

subject: Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) identified 9 affected females, 7 of whom had truncating variants; 3 of these 7 had macrocephaly and 4 did not. Macrocephaly was discordant in 2 mother-daughter pairs, and learning disabilities appeared milder in females. X-inactivation studies were available for only 3 females and did not match the phenotype.

subject: Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) found macrocephaly in 70% of individuals with truncating variants. However, 3 individuals with truncating variants lacked brain overgrowth and 4 with missense variants had it, so the feature was not restricted to putative loss-of-function variants. Individuals with CNV deletions that included SMARCA1 did not have macrocephaly. Three of the 4 missense variants associated with macrocephaly were in the HSS domain.

subject: Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) identified the SMARCA1 variants by trio exome sequencing (23 families) or genome sequencing (3 families), with families ascertained partly through MatchMaker Exchange. There were 25 unique variants: 7 nonsense, 3 frameshift and 15 missense. All were predicted deleterious, and each was very rare or absent in gnomAD (allele frequency 8.303 x 10(-7) or lower; p.Met432Thr was seen in 4 alleles). Sixteen variants were in the ATPase (12) or HSS (4) domains.

object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) considered SMARCA1 variants in 7 additional families likely non-causative. These included p.Val384Met (c.1150G-A) in 3 families; this variant had previously been reported in familial schizophrenia and was present in gnomAD in 16 alleles, including 7 hemizygotes. Others were p.Pro537Leu (c.1610C-T) in 2 families, which also had a high gnomAD frequency, and p.Gly38Val, found together with a de novo 5p15 duplication.

Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) searched DECIPHER and found 72 CNVs encompassing SMARCA1 (44% deletions, 56% duplications). Carriers often had developmental delay, intellectual disability or delayed speech, but the phenotype was hard to attribute to SMARCA1 because most CNVs were larger than 10 Mb. Individuals with deletions did not have macrocephaly.

subject: Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) performed genome-wide DNA methylation analysis of peripheral blood from 19 individuals with SMARCA1 variants and found a predominantly hypomethylated profile defined by 232 probes compared with controls. Males and females each also showed sex-specific hypomethylated profiles. The authors concluded that these changes were not robust enough to count as an episignature.

subject: Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) expressed FLAG-tagged SMARCA1 variants in U2OS cells. The p.Arg253Ter, p.Arg259Gly, p.Arg751Gln and p.Glu771Lys variants all produced stable proteins that localized to the nucleus. The Arg253Ter variant produced a stable 35-kD truncated protein at a somewhat lower level, and it was also found in the cytoplasm. The authors suggested that some truncating variants generate truncated proteins with hypomorphic or dominant-negative activity.

subject: Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) found that Smarca1-null mice were viable and had little change in brain size, only slight reductions in a few regions, with normal progenitor populations and cortical lamination. The mice were more active in the dark cycle but otherwise behaved normally on tests of locomotion, social interaction, anxiety, learning and memory. In Smarca1-null cerebellum, SMARCA5 co-immunoprecipitated with CECR2, which the authors suggested reflects functional compensation by SMARCA5.

subject: Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) compared single and double knockouts of the NURF components Smarca1, Smarca5 and Bptf in mice. Bptf knockout caused the most severe cortical hypoplasia, and no double mutant was more severe. Smarca1ex6del mice, which express an internally truncated protein, had a total brain area 10% larger than controls, but this enlargement was lost when Smarca5 was also ablated. The authors proposed that Smarca5 compensates for complete loss of Smarca1 but not when a mutant SMARCA1 protein is produced, which may act as a dominant negative.

subject: Mirzaa et al. (2025)
object: Mirzaa et al. (2025) proposed that SMARCA1 variants associated with macrocephaly lack remodeling activity and act in a dominant-negative fashion, whereas variants not associated with macrocephaly may be functional hypomorphs. In their view, all of these variants alter NURF composition and function in the developing brain.
